justification: No article reports LRRTM2 variants identified in ASD probands. The evidence is biological/mechanistic: LRRTM2 is a postsynaptic neurexin ligand that cooperates with neuroligins in glutamatergic synapse development (PMID 20519524), and it is discussed as part of the neurexin–neuroligin–LRRTM synaptic adhesion network implicated in ASD/schizophrenia (PMID 21155806). The NRXN2/NRXN1 truncation study (PMID 21424692) uses LRRTM2 only as an in vitro binding partner assay, not as a mutated gene in patients. The 5q31 microdeletion report (PMID 23326251) proposes LRRTM2 as a candidate for ID/DD, but the deletion spans multiple genes and targeted sequencing of 330 ID/DD patients found no relevant LRRTM2 mutations — a negative human genetic result, and for ID/DD rather than ASD. Therefore the relationship is best characterized as hypothesized on pathway/functional grounds.

justification: All substantive CHRNA1 literature here concerns the muscle nicotinic acetylcholine receptor alpha subunit and neuromuscular junction disorders: congenital myasthenic syndromes, fetal akinesia deformation sequence/multiple pterygium syndrome, and autoimmune myasthenia gravis (PMIDs 20157724, 18252226, 22728938, 17687331, 22482962). None of these phenotypes is epilepsy or a recognized epilepsy precursor. The only article even mentioning epilepsy is the porcine congenital ataxia/spastic paresis mapping study (PMID 17868079), where CHRNA1 was listed as a positional candidate alongside ion channel genes and then explicitly excluded — and that work is in pigs, not humans. There are therefore no human genetic variant data, and no functional or animal data (zebrafish CHRNA1 work, PMIDs 15128655, 16249237, concerns muscle development), linking CHRNA1 to seizures. A small residual weight is given to "hypothesized" only because of the generic cholinergic-receptor/ion-channel rationale invoked in the candidate-gene screen.

justification: No article reports GRIA2 sequence variants identified in autism probands with replication; the only human autism-specific genetic finding is a single case report of a large 19 Mb interstitial 4q deletion spanning ~33 genes including AMPA2/GRIA2 (PMID 15090072), which cannot single out GRIA2 and therefore cannot support "Established." Other human genetic papers involving GRIA2 concern schizophrenia (PMID 22094384, 18163426), lithium response in bipolar disorder (PMID 19448189), ALS/MND (PMID 20409611, 16523673), or multigene CNVs in mental retardation cohorts (PMID 19623214, 20358617) — none demonstrate an autism association. The GRIP1 study (PMID 21383172) implicates a GluA2-interacting scaffold protein, not GRIA2 variants, in autism, and the Epac2 work (PMID 19734897, 21115118) shows GluR2/3 removal from spines as an ASD-relevant mechanism; both provide biological/pathway plausibility rather than direct genetic evidence. Thus the balance favors "Hypothesized" (strong mechanistic/synaptic rationale, animal and in vitro data) with meaningful residual probability for "Existing" based on the single hemizygous-deletion autism case highlighting GRIA2 as a candidate.

justification: Every article provided concerns MYH2 (fast myosin heavy chain IIa) in the context of skeletal muscle disease: autosomal dominant/recessive myosin myopathies, inclusion body myopathy 3, external ophthalmoplegia, and sporadic inclusion body myositis. None of the papers mention autism spectrum disorder, neurodevelopmental phenotypes, behavior, or brain expression, and no genetic association, functional, or animal-model data link MYH2 to ASD. The model organism work (C. elegans, Drosophila, mouse) is entirely about muscle contractility and thick filament structure, providing no biological pathway relevant to ASD. Therefore the evidence base supports only a "Novel" designation for the MYH2–ASD relationship as of 2012.

justification: The only available article (PMID 20035503) concerns Parkinson's disease, reporting differential expression of TRAPPC4 in substantia nigra neurons and association analysis that ultimately implicated PDXK, not TRAPPC4, and makes no mention of epilepsy or seizures. There is no clinical, genetic, functional, or animal-model evidence linking TRAPPC4 variants or biology to epilepsy in this literature set. The vesicle-transport function mentioned is too generic to constitute a specific mechanistic hypothesis for epilepsy here. Therefore the relationship is best described as Novel, with only a small residual allowance for a vague biological rationale.

justification: No article in this set reports KCNC1 variants in epilepsy patients; the only human mutation screening (Usher syndrome 1C candidate gene analysis, PMIDs 9041816, 9445488) found no mutations and concerns a non-epilepsy phenotype. The relationship is supported only indirectly by biology: Kv3.1 mediates fast-spiking firing in GABAergic interneurons (PMIDs 18708127, 18775767, 21440618), is the target of the antiepileptic drug levetiracetam (PMID 20065495), and is implicated in 4-aminopyridine-induced ictogenesis and expression changes in chronic epileptic rats (PMID 17942314). Notably, the Kcnc1-null mouse showed motor and muscle deficits but explicitly no spontaneous seizures (PMID 9037088), weakening but not eliminating the mechanistic rationale. This profile fits "Hypothesized" — plausible biological/pathway and animal-model relevance without any human genetic evidence — with some residual probability of "Novel" given the negative knockout seizure phenotype.
